newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela worried about chemical war reports.
newsitem.headline: Mandela worried about chemical war reports.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela expressed concern on Tuesday at reports of a secret South African chemical warfare project during the apartheid era, saying they could be the "tip of the iceberg".

Allegations that South Africa developed an advanced chemical war programme, not just the defensive measures it has acknowledged, emerged after former army scientist Wouter Basson -- who played a leading role in the programme -- was arrested in Pretoria last month on charges of dealing in the banned "rave" drug Ecstasy.
His bail application last week was initially heard in camera because of fears that state secrets could be revealed, but newspapers brought legal action to have the hearings opened to the public.
They quoted a national intelligence agent as telling the bail hearing that highly classified documents on chemical warfare had been seized from the home of Basson and a colleague.

The agent said Basson had contacts in Libya, raising the possibility that he had sold chemical warfare secrets to Tripoli, and that the intelligence agencies of several foreign countries would like to either kill or abduct him because of his knowledge
"If this expertise fell into the wrong hands, it would be a disaster," the papers quoted the South African agent as saying in court.

Mandela, talking to reporters on Tuesday, said he had been told before the April 1994 democratic elections that the United States and Britain had pressed South Africa to drop its chemical warfare programme and that it had acceded to the request.
"Of course these (Basson) revelations, I'm sure are going to be investigated very thoroughly...
"It's a matter of great concern. It may be just the tip of the iceberg, there may be a lot that has not been revealed," Mandela said.
In 1995 the South African weapons agency Armscor invited reporters to tour a chemical war facility outside Johannesburg where gas masks and other defensive items are developed.
Armscor said minute quantities of substances such as mustard gas were produced to test the equipment, but that this was the limit of South Africa's chemical weapons output.
